title: Work as Zen
hook: an old cook drying mushrooms in the hot sun: in Zen monasteries, the work period is practice too

segments.voice: Yesterday: shoshin. Your line was beginner's mind. What did you do once as if for the first time? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-six.

Midday, a Chinese monastery, and the sun is brutal. An old monk with a bent back is out in the courtyard with no hat, spreading mushrooms to dry, sweating. A visitor from Japan, Dogen, the same Dogen we met at the start of the week, stops and asks: why not have a helper do this? The old cook answers, in effect: other people are not me. And why not wait until it's cooler? If not now, when? Dogen writes that he had nothing to say back. He tells this story in his instructions for the monastery cook. Today's word is what that old man was doing.
screen: `AN OLD COOK, DRYING MUSHROOMS.` → `OTHERS ARE NOT ME.` → `IF NOT NOW, WHEN?`

segments.voice: Samu is the Japanese Zen word for the work period: cleaning, cooking, sweeping, weeding, done as practice. First, what it is. In a Zen monastery, the day isn't only sitting. There are set times for physical work, and the work is treated as part of the training, not a break from it. Often it's done without chatter, with the same attention the cushion asks for. Second, an old saying. Tradition says the Chinese teacher Baizhang kept working in the fields even when he was old. His students, worried for him, hid his tools. He then refused to eat, and said, as the story goes: a day without work is a day without food. Whether or not it happened just that way, Zen still repeats the saying. Third, the cook's answer. Back to the mushrooms. Other people are not me. The old cook wasn't refusing help out of pride. He meant that his practice was this task, in his own hands. Sending it to someone else would be sending away his own practice. And if not now, when: the moment to pay attention is the one you're in, even if it's hot. Fourth, the ordinary Tuesday part. Just sitting, koans, beginner's mind: this week has been about the cushion. Samu takes it off the cushion. Washing a pan can be zazen with your hands moving. In his instructions for the cook, Dogen asks, in paraphrase, that rice and water be handled with the care you'd give your own eyes. Nobody has to live in a monastery to try that with a sink full of dishes.
screen: `SAMU: THE WORK PERIOD AS PRACTICE.` · `A DAY WITHOUT WORK, A DAY WITHOUT FOOD.` · `OTHERS ARE NOT ME.` · `THE CUSHION, WITH YOUR HANDS MOVING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a little samu. Find one small thing within reach that needs care. A cup to wash, a table to wipe, a stack of papers, a pair of shoes to line up. Do it slowly, with your full attention. Feel the weight of the thing, the water's temperature, the cloth under your hand. When your mind runs ahead to what's next, come back to this one motion. If you're somewhere you can't move, tidy one thing in your pocket or bag. If you have more time later, ten minutes of cleaning this way is a good next step. The bell holds the time.
Samu. The Zen work period, cleaning, cooking, tending, done as practice, with the same attention as sitting. Today's word.
Your line: work is practice. Today, choose one chore you'd usually rush, and give it the old cook's answer: not someone else, and not later. This one, now. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: In Zen monasteries and practice centers, residents keep a daily work period, cleaning, cooking or gardening, often in silence, as part of their training.

notes: Editor pass: cut 'young' (an age claim not needed); 'the saying stuck as a rule for monastic life' softened to 'Zen still repeats the saying' (no historical claim); removed the repeated 'four ways' teach frame.

The mushroom-drying story is paraphrased from Tenzo Kyokun; confirm details (midday heat, no hat, Dogen's questions, 'others are not me', 'if not now, when'). The cook's age, given in the text, is left out under the claims rule.
Baizhang's saying and the hidden-tools story are given as 'tradition says' / 'as the story goes'; confirm the attribution is fairly hedged.
Dogen's instruction to handle rice and water with the care given one's own eyes is paraphrased from Tenzo Kyokun; confirm.
Outline practice is ten minutes of mindful cleaning; the sit is two, so ten minutes is offered as a later option.
